narrative:
The model estimates you have a 13% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. First, having no past class failures actually worked in your favor and pulled the prediction toward passing. Second, your clear desire to pursue higher education also pushed strongly toward a passing outcome. However, the single most influential factor was your limited weekly study time of less than two hours. This is considerably lower than the majority of students who passed (most studied 2–5 hours), and it pushed the prediction toward failing enough to outweigh the protective effects of the other two features.

Because your study habits created the strongest pull toward a negative outcome, this is the area with the greatest potential for change. Consider increasing your dedicated study time, perhaps by setting a realistic schedule of at least two to three hours most weekdays. Small, consistent improvements in how you prepare could shift your trajectory and reduce the need for remedial courses next year.
